RagShortTexts: The heraldic rule of tincture barred metal on metal, ensuring shields remained recognizable.

Variants.Content: Once a knight's face disappeared behind an enclosed great helm, his shield and surcoat became the only reliable way to tell one man from another on a crowded field. Heraldry grew into a discipline with its own rules, and the heralds who enforced it looked for order in every painted field. The Rule of Tincture forbade placing metal upon metal, such as gold or silver, and colour upon colour, such as red, blue, black, green or purple. Heralds kept armorial rolls that recorded paternal lines, cadency marks that distinguished younger sons, and the designs of banners carried in the field. A coat that broke these rules could be disputed in court, so accurate painting and careful record-keeping protected a family's claim to its arms.

The lion, fleur-de-lis or eagle on a heater shield stood for ancestral blood, often spilled in holy enterprise. A man who took up another family's bearings risked trial before a heraldic court, where a conviction could mean a public breaking of swords and the loss of his claim.

In the press of battle a soldier reads the colours on lances and trappings, since that is how friend and foe are told apart. When the golden leopard banner moves forward, your line moves with it. If the azure fleur-de-lis falls, the command has broken and the men around you will scatter. Keep near the standard and listen for the word.
